lead: At a fixed temperature, a solid adsorbent in contact with a fluid reaches equilibrium when the rate of molecules sticking to the surface equals the rate leaving it. The equilibrium solid loading q (mg/g) plotted against fluid concentration C (mg/L) is the adsorption isotherm. It answers a practical question: for a given feed concentration, how much solute will a gram of carbon, silica or resin hold? Designers use it for drinking-water treatment, dye removal, sugar decolourisation and solvent recovery.
prereq: You need: 6.1 Adsorption principles and adsorbents for surface area, pores and capacity.

blocks.text: An isotherm is measured by shaking known masses of adsorbent with solutions of different initial concentration until equilibrium. q is the mass of solute adsorbed per mass of dry adsorbent (mg/g). C, often written Ce, is the remaining solute concentration in the fluid (mg/L). Each point is one equilibrium pair (C, q). The same idea applies to a gas; then use partial pressure p (Pa or bar) in place of C.
q = q_max K_L C / (1 + K_L C)
blocks.where: q is solid loading (mg solute per g dry solid); C is fluid concentration at equilibrium (mg/L); q_max is monolayer capacity (mg/g); K_L is affinity constant (L/mg).

blocks.text: Langmuir model assumes adsorption stops at one monolayer. Sites are identical, each holds one molecule, and adsorbed molecules do not interact. At low C many sites are free, so q rises almost linearly with C. At high C the monolayer fills and q approaches q_max. K_L measures how strongly the solute binds: a larger K_L reaches the plateau at a lower C.

blocks.where: Plot C/q against C: slope = 1/q_max; intercept = 1/(q_max K_L).

blocks.text: To find the constants, plot C/q against C. The line has slope 1/q_max and intercept 1/(q_max K_L). Invert the slope to get q_max; divide intercept into 1/q_max to get K_L. If the data do not form a straight line, Langmuir is only an approximation.
Many real surfaces are heterogeneous: some sites bind strongly, others weakly. The Freundlich isotherm is empirical and allows that spread. It does not assume a monolayer and has no finite plateau.

blocks.where: K_F is capacity constant ((mg/g)(L/mg)^(1/n)); n is dimensionless heterogeneity index; C in mg/L.

blocks.text: K_F is a capacity constant; its units are (mg/g)(L/mg)^(1/n) and depend on 1/n. n is a dimensionless number that describes how steeply loading rises with concentration. For favourable adsorption, 1/n lies between 0 and 1, so n > 1; the surface is easily loaded at low C and more C gives diminishing extra loading.
log q = log K_F + (1/n) log C
blocks.where: Plot log q against log C: slope = 1/n; intercept = log K_F.

blocks.text: Plot log q against log C. Slope = 1/n, intercept = log K_F. Use base 10 or natural logs consistently. Freundlich fits a limited concentration range; it cannot predict a true saturation capacity, so do not use it far outside the measured range.

Physisorption is exothermic. At fixed C, raising temperature shifts equilibrium toward desorption, so q usually falls. The constants q_max, K_L, K_F and n are therefore tied to the temperature at which they were measured. Chemisorption can behave differently because a chemical bond must form; it may need heat and can increase with temperature, but it is not simple physical adsorption.

For a gas, loading depends on the partial pressure of the adsorbate, not total pressure. Raising total pressure at fixed mole fraction raises partial pressure and hence q. Raising only an inert gas pressure has little effect. A pressure-swing adsorber uses this: high pressure loads the bed, low pressure strips it.

An isotherm is favourable when it is concave downward: a large q is reached at small C. Such a curve gives a good driving force in a fixed bed and a sharp breakthrough, discussed in 6.3. A linear isotherm is intermediate; a concave-up isotherm is unfavourable and needs much more adsorbent.

figure.caption: The curve is q = 40 × 1.5 × Ce / (1 + 1.5 × Ce) at 25 °C. The marked points are the two answers in the worked example.

spec.aria: A rising Langmuir curve that flattens near 40 mg/g, with two marked points at Ce 2 mg/L and q 30 mg/g and at Ce 0.667 mg/L and q 20 mg/g.

examples.question: At 25 °C, a dye on activated carbon follows the Langmuir isotherm with q_max = 40 mg/g and K_L = 1.5 L/mg. (a) Find q at Ce = 2.0 mg/L. (b) Find Ce when q = 20 mg/g.
steps: Langmuir equation: q = q_max K_L C / (1 + K_L C).
(a) Put q_max = 40 mg/g, K_L = 1.5 L/mg, C = 2.0 mg/L. K_L C = 3.0 (dimensionless). Numerator = 40 × 3.0 = 120 mg/g. Denominator = 1 + 3.0 = 4.0. q = 120 / 4.0 = 30 mg/g.
examples.answer: At 25 °C, q = 30 mg/g at Ce = 2.0 mg/L; Ce = 0.667 mg/L when q = 20 mg/g.
examples.check:
qmax = 40.0
KL = 1.5
Ce = 2.0
q = qmax * KL * Ce / (1 + KL * Ce)
print(round(q, 1))
q_target = 20.0
Ce2 = q_target / (KL * (qmax - q_target))
print(round(Ce2, 3))

traps: Reading the intercept of the Langmuir plot C/q versus C as q_max. It is 1/q_max; invert it.
Mixing units: q in mg/g uses mass solute per mass dry solid, C in mg/L, and K_L in L/mg. Convert before multiplying.
Treating Freundlich n as q_max. Freundlich has no plateau; n only sets the exponent.
Applying a 25 °C isotherm to a 60 °C stream. Constants change with temperature; physisorption usually falls on heating.
For a gas, using total pressure in place of adsorbate partial pressure. Loading follows the partial pressure.

quiz.q: Define q_max and state the unit of K_L in the Langmuir equation.
quiz.a: q_max is the monolayer capacity, the maximum mass adsorbed per mass dry solid (mg/g). K_L is the affinity constant; when C is in mg/L, K_L has units L/mg.

quiz.q: Why does the Langmuir isotherm flatten at high C?
quiz.a: All monolayer sites become occupied. Further increase in C cannot raise q beyond q_max, so the curve approaches q_max.

quiz.q: In a Freundlich linear plot of log q against log C, what are slope and intercept?
quiz.a: Slope = 1/n; intercept = log K_F. Invert the slope to get n; take antilog of intercept to get K_F.

quiz.q: A carbon follows Langmuir with q_max = 50 mg/g and K_L = 0.8 L/mg. Find q at C = 5 mg/L.
Freundlich K_F = 10 (mg/g)(L/mg)^(1/n), n = 2. Find q at C = 4 mg/L and at C = 8 mg/L.
quiz.a: q = 10 × 4^(1/2) = 20 mg/g. At 8 mg/L, q = 10 × 8^(1/2) = 28.3 mg/g. Doubling C raises q by √2, not 2.

quiz.q: Carbon A: q_max = 100 mg/g, K_L = 0.1 L/mg. Carbon B: q_max = 40 mg/g, K_L = 2 L/mg. Which is better at C = 0.1 mg/L and at C = 10 mg/L?
quiz.a: At C = 0.1, A gives about 0.99 mg/g, B about 6.67 mg/g; B wins by affinity. At C = 10, A gives 50 mg/g, B about 38.1 mg/g; A wins by capacity.

quiz.q: A plant uses a 25 °C isotherm to design a column fed at 60 °C. What error is likely and why?
quiz.a: The design will overpredict loading. Physisorption is exothermic, so at 60 °C q at fixed C is lower; the bed will break through earlier unless a 60 °C isotherm is used.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real surfaces often need multilayer or heterogeneous models: BET for multilayers and Sips or Toth for mixed behaviour. Competitive adsorption matters when several solutes share sites, as in water treatment. Pressure-swing and temperature-swing cycles turn these isotherms into oxygen concentrators and adsorption chillers. Search for BET isotherm, Sips isotherm and adsorption chiller if you want the next step.
